div.head: Af 4
div.ab: V. Gif hwa ymb cyninges feorh sierwe, ðurh hine oððe ðurh wreccena feormunge oððe his manna, sie he his feores scyldig ⁊ ealles þæs ðe he age.
V. Gif hwa ymb cyninges feorh syrwie, þurh hine oððe þurh wrecena feormunge oððe his manna, sy he his feores scyldig ⁊ ealles þæs ðe he age.
Be cynincges swicdome. Gyf hwá ymb cyninges feorh syrwie, ðurh hine oððe wrecena feormunge oððe his manna, sy he his feores scyldig ⁊ ealles ðæs þe he age.
Si quis per se uel susceptam uel suspectam personam de morte regis tractet, uitę sue reus sit et omnium quę habebit.
[Be cynincges swicdome.] Gif hwa ymb cyninges feorh sierwe, ðurh hine oððe ðurh wreccena feormunge oððe his manna, sie he his feores scyldig ⁊ ealles þæs ðe he age.
{V} Gif swa ymb cyninges feorh sierwe, ðurh hine oððe ðurh wreccena feormunge oððe his manna, sie he his feores scyldig ⁊ ealles þæs ðe he age.

Wenn jemand dem Leben des Königs nachstellt, durch sich oder durch Beherbergung Verbannter oder der Mannen eines von ihnen, sei er [des Verlustes] seines Lebens und alles dessen, was er besitzt, schuldig.
If someone plots against the king’s life, by himself or by harbouring outlaws or the men of one of them, let him be liable [to lose] his life and everything that he possesses.
If anyone plots against the life of the king, either on his own account, or by harbouring outlaws, or men belonging to [the king] himself, he shall forfeit his life and all he possesses.
If anyone plots against the king’s life, directly or by harbouring his exiles or his men, he is liable to forfeit his life and all that he owns.
If someone plots against the king’s life, either by his own actions, or by the harboring of those who have been banished or of his men, let him be liable for his life and all that he owns.

note.label: evokes
note.quote: This evokes the terms of Alfred’s treason law (2), decreeing death and forfeiture for the ‘harbouring of exiles’

note.seg: Überschriften roth. Ich drucke sie fett, wo sie nicht aus obiger Rubrikenliste S. 16 ff. stammen.
Headings in red. I print them in bold where they do not come from the list of rubrics above, p. 16 ff.
before it, written above later, eard

‘Über Verrat am König’ B. Dessen Überschriften weichen teilweise von obiger Rubrikenliste des Archetyps ab und sind erst um 1100 entstanden; s. Einl. 13. Er wählt für ‘Verrat’ nicht das Wort des Textes, sondern ein moderneres

‘On treason against the king’ B. Its rubrics differ in part from the above list of rubrics of the archetype and arose only c. 1100; see Introduction 13. For ‘treason’ it chooses not the word of the text but a more modern one
Vgl. Gl Hochverrat 2—4a. Diesen Satz benutzt V Atr 30
Cf. Gl Hochverrat 2—4a. This sentence is used by V Atr 30
‘in eigener Person’ Schmid, im Ggs. zur Begünstigung (vgl. Gl 6—8), die ebenso wie das Verbrechen selbst bestraft wird
‘in his own person’ Schmid, in contrast to abetting (cf. Gl 6—8), which is punished in the same way as the crime itself

Q übersetzt zu frei, mit kanonistischer Färbung. — ‘Landesflüchtiger’ B cor. Dieses Wort scheint sonst nicht belegt; vermutlich hatte ohne vorgesetztes eard- das Wort wrecca (vgl. Gl friedlos 11) den Sinn des Verbanntseins verloren und ging (wie dt. elend) zur Bed. wretch über

Q translates too freely, with a canonistic colouring. — ‘fugitive from the land’ B cor. This word seems not to be attested elsewhere; presumably without the prefixed eard- the word wrecca (cf. Gl friedlos 11) had lost the sense of being banished and passed (like German elend) to the meaning wretch
‘his (seiner)’ zu wörtlich Thorpe; ‘derselben’ sachlich richtig Schmid
‘his (seiner)’ Thorpe, too literally; ‘derselben’ Schmid, correct in substance

note.label: wreccena
note.seg: om. þurh. B. eard added above the line in 16th cent.

i.e. men in the king’s service, who are plotting secretly against the king’s life. Schmid and Liebermann take his in connection with wreccena, and translate ‘their men’ or ‘men belonging to one of them’; but such a construction seems hardly possible.

note.label: men
note.seg: Liebermann takes this to mean the men of any one of the exiles, but the natural antecedent is the king, as Attenborough takes it. Presumably disloyal men are meant.
